value.overview: The Yellow-eared Toucanet (Selenidera spectabilis) is a medium-sized toucan of humid forests in Central and northwestern South America. It is named for the long yellow ear patch shown by adult males. This forest-canopy species usually occurs alone, in pairs, or in small groups and helps disperse seeds while feeding on fruit. Costa Rica is an important part of its northern range, where the species is resident but makes seasonal movements to lower elevations after breeding.
value.classification: The Yellow-eared Toucanet belongs to the toucan family Ramphastidae and the order Piciformes. It is one of the sexually dimorphic toucanets in the genus Selenidera.
value.identification: Adults have a predominantly black throat, breast, and belly, reddish undertail coverts, chestnut thighs, and yellow to orange markings on the flanks. The bill is multicolored, with yellowish upper areas, darker edges and tip, and a reddish interior. The male has a conspicuous yellow ear patch behind the eye; the female lacks this patch and has a more extensively chestnut-brown head and hindneck. Juveniles are duller and show less strongly developed facial and flank markings.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Honduras through Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid forested slopes on the Caribbean side throughout much of the country, and occurs locally on the Pacific side, especially in the Cordillera de Guanacaste. It favors mature, tall wet forest and dense-canopied secondary growth, usually from about 100 to 1,200 meters, with some records reaching approximately 1,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica, but many individuals move downslope after breeding. These seasonal movements commonly occur from about September through January, sometimes continuing into March, and are not considered long-distance migration.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from February through May, especially between about 300 and 1,200 meters. The nest is placed in an old woodpecker cavity in a dead tree that is not yet badly decayed, typically about 6 to 20 meters above the ground. Pairs are the usual breeding unit. The eggs have not been reliably described in the available Costa Rican sources.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms the main part of the diet, and the toucanet usually forages in the middle and upper levels of forest vegetation. It also takes animal prey such as insects, lizards, frogs, bird eggs, and nestlings. By swallowing fruit and later passing the seeds, it contributes to seed dispersal. It may descend into nearby secondary growth or shaded clearings when food resources are available there.
value.behavior: Yellow-eared Toucanets are generally seen alone or in pairs, sometimes in small groups of two to four. After breeding, groups of four to eight may form. They are active in the forest canopy and can be difficult to detect despite their bright markings. Individuals use repeated calls during social interactions and when defending a nest or territory, often moving or bobbing the head while vocalizing.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not well quantified. The species remains fairly widespread, although local populations may be affected by the loss and fragmentation of mature humid forest.
